<!-- slide 96 -->
# Building a Plot {.divider}

[A scatter, step by step · Day 01]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 97 -->
## Building a Plot · The Data {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · what we're plotting]{.eyebrow}

### How the data loads

`load_coexpression()` returns one row per sample: two gene expression values plus the tissue it came from. Three tissues, Leaf / Root / Seed.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()        # sample, tissue, gene_x, gene_y
co.head(3)
```


<!-- slide 98 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 1 — The Canvas {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Canvas

We'll build a **scatter**: gene Y against gene X, one dot per sample. Start with a **figure** and an **axes**, then frame the axes before drawing anything.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "3-6"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))   # one figure, one axes
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")     # frame the axes before drawing
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 99 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 2 — Load & Plot Data {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Data

Load the samples and drop them onto the canvas with `ax.scatter()`. One dot per sample, default colour for now.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2,4,10"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()                     # sample, tissue, gene_x, gene_y

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
ax.scatter(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, color=GREY, s=50, alpha=.8)   # one dot per sample
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 100 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 3 — Colour by Tissue {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Colour

Loop over the tissues, one pass each, one palette colour each. Colour now carries real signal, the tissues separate.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "10-14"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}   # one colour per tissue
for tissue, c in pal.items():
    g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
    ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")     # name the tissues
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 101 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 4 — Polish & Labels {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Polish

A single linear fit across all samples summarises the trend. Compute slope and intercept, draw it in red, and let the title state what we found.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "14-17"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
for tissue, c in pal.items():
    g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
    ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)             # single linear fit
xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)   # draw it in red
ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")  # state the finding
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 102 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 5 — Style Once, Reuse Everywhere {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 5 · House style

Bundle your spine and grid choices into one block and apply it. The per-axes spine code disappears, every plot inherits the same look.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "6-13"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {                                    # the house style, defined ONCE
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):                  # apply it: no per-axes spine code
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 103 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 6 — Transparency {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 6 · Alpha

Lower the dot opacity. Where samples pile up along the line the colour deepens, so density reads instead of one solid mass.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "21"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)   # lower alpha: density shows
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 104 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 7 — Drop the Vertical Grid {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 7 · Grid

Keep the horizontal gridlines as value guides, drop the verticals. Fewer competing lines, the eye reads the y values cleanly.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "25"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)                     # keep horizontal guides, drop verticals
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")

```


<!-- slide 105 -->
## Building a Plot · Step 8 — Point At It {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack · building a figure]{.eyebrow}

### 8 · Arrow

Find the sample furthest above the fit, then aim a curved `annotate` arrow at it. The `rad` bends the arrow so it comes in from the side instead of crossing the dot.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "26-31"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)
    co["resid"] = co.gene_y - (m * co.gene_x + b)   # distance from the fit
    hot = co.loc[co.resid.idxmax()]                 # furthest sample above it
    ax.annotate(f"{hot.tissue} outlier", xy=(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y),
                xytext=(hot.gene_x - 3.2, hot.gene_y + 2.0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.3"))   # curved callout
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.text(0.0, 1.05, "co-expression across three tissues",         # italic subtitle
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, color=MUTED, style="italic")
    fig.text(0.5, -0.04, "Source: load_coexpression() · demo data",  # caption
             ha="center", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Build in layers, then refine with **properties**: transparency for density, a lighter grid, a curved arrow plus a white edge to single one point out, and a layered **title / subtitle / caption** to say what it means.
:::

<!-- slide 109 -->
## Exercise — Solution & the Catch {.smaller}

[Exercise · solution]{.eyebrow}

### r is high — but here that is an artifact

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The recipe runs and prints a strong-looking r. The catch: in this toy dataset
`expression` was **built** as `0.8 * log2fc + noise`, so the correlation is
baked in, and `group` is assigned at random. The number is real; the biology
is not. Always ask what generated the data before trusting an r.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "10-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_scatter_demo

df = load_scatter_demo()

with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.6))
    ax.scatter(df.log2fc, df.expression, color=GREY, s=45, alpha=.7)
    r = np.corrcoef(df.log2fc, df.expression)[0, 1]   # Pearson r
    ax.text(0.04, 0.93, f"r = {r:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
    ax.set_ylabel("expression")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.exercise}
[Exercise · the lesson]{.xl}
A high r only means two columns move together. Here they move together **by construction**. Correlation is a description, not a discovery.
:::

<!-- slide 110 -->
# Ternary Plots {.divider}

[Compositional data · three parts that sum to one]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 111 -->
## Ternary · The Data {.smaller}

[Genomics · compositional data]{.eyebrow}

### Three ancestry fractions per individual, summing to one

Each individual's ancestry splits across three populations and the fractions sum to 1. We simulate that with a Dirichlet draw: mostly-A, mostly-B, mostly-C, plus some evenly admixed.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
import numpy as np, pandas as pd

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])
adm = pd.DataFrame(comp, columns=["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"]).round(3)
adm.head(4)
```


<!-- slide 112 -->
## Ternary · Step 1 — The Triangle {.smaller}

[Genomics · compositional data]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Frame

`ternary_diagram` draws the triangle, gridlines, and ticks for you. Three corners, one per population. Near a corner means mostly that population, the centre means evenly admixed.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1,8"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)        # fixed seed -> same points every step
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)   # frame, gridlines, ticks
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 113 -->
## Ternary · Step 2 — The Points {.smaller}

[Genomics · compositional data]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Scatter

`td.scatter` takes the whole `comp` array, one row per individual. It places each point by its three fractions automatically. One colour for now.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)
td.scatter(vector=comp, c=GREY, s=28, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)   # one dot per individual
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 114 -->
## Ternary · Step 3 — Colour by Population {.smaller}

[Genomics · compositional data]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Colour

Colour each point by its **dominant** population (`argmax` of the three fractions). The three corner clusters light up; the admixed individuals stay near the middle.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "7,10"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

cols = np.array([GREEN, BLUE, AMBER])[comp.argmax(1)]   # colour by dominant population
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)
td.scatter(vector=comp, c=cols, s=28, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Three parts that sum to one belong in a **triangle**. Corners are pure ancestry, the centre is admixture, and `argmax` colouring reveals the dominant population at a glance.
:::
